results.title: Generative AI in Higher Education | by Michael Buehler | Jan, 2026
results.content: While advocates argue chatbots can save teachers time and personalize learning, critics warn of harms including diminished critical thinking, misinformation, and expanded AI-assisted cheating, with UNICEF urging caution based on past classroom tech disappointments such as “One Laptop per Child.” The article highlights national efforts in Estonia and Iceland that emphasize AI literacy, controlled pilots, and research partnerships, including Estonia’s approach of tuning bots to respond with questions rather than direct answers and Iceland’s decision to keep student access limited while teachers experiment under study. **Summary:** Charles Logan argues that ed-tech marketing, especially around “AI,” relies on mystifying language that obscures human design, institutional power, and accountability, drawing on Emily Tucker’s “Baldwin Test” and Emily Bender’s warnings about ceding power to those “behind the curtain.” He outlines the test’s four commitments (specific technical description, naming transparency gaps, naming responsible corporations, and attributing agency to human actors) and then proposes three education-specific extensions: naming the technology’s theory of learning, describing its effects on pedagogy, and highlighting environmental impacts.
